section.title: Honesty in Daily Life
section.sectionRationale: Part of the first Solomonic collection, 10:1 to 22:16, this chapter clusters proverbs on the folly of drink and quarreling, the LORD who searches the human spirit and weighs every scale, and the honest dealing that marks the wise from the fraudulent.
section.thesis: Honesty in weights, words, and work matters because the LORD's lamp searches every inmost being and no one can claim a pure heart on his own, so wisdom means honest dealing, restrained speech, patient trust, and dependence on the God who alone tests what is hidden.
section.frameNote: Six clusters: wine, strife, and the honorable resolution of disputes; the king's discernment and the heart's hidden depths; honest weights and the LORD's searching lamp; food gained by fraud and plans made by counsel; cursing parents and the peril of rash vows; the glory of youth, age, and the king's throne secured by loyalty.

verses.text: Wine is a mocker, strong drink is a brawler, and whoever is led astray by them is not wise.
The terror of a king is like the roar of a lion; whoever provokes him forfeits his own life.
It is honorable for a man to resolve a dispute, but any fool will quarrel.
The slacker does not plow in season; at harvest time he looks, but nothing is there.

units.label: The king's discernment and the heart's depths

verses.text: The intentions of a man's heart are deep waters, but a man of understanding draws them out.
Many a man proclaims his loving devotion, but who can find a trustworthy man?
The righteous man walks with integrity; blessed are his children after him.
A king who sits on a throne to judge sifts out all evil with his eyes.
Who can say, "I have kept my heart pure; I am cleansed from my sin"?

units.label: Honest weights and the LORD's searching lamp

verses.text: Differing weights and unequal measures, both are detestable to the LORD.
Even a young man is known by his actions, whether his conduct is pure and upright.
Ears that hear and eyes that see, the LORD has made them both.
Do not love sleep, or you will grow poor; open your eyes, and you will have plenty of food.
"Worthless, worthless!" says the buyer, but on the way out, he gloats.
There is an abundance of gold and rubies, but lips of knowledge are a rare treasure.
Take the garment of the one who posts security for a stranger; get collateral if it is for a foreigner.
Food gained by fraud is sweet to a man, but later his mouth is full of gravel.
Set plans by consultation, and wage war under sound guidance.
He who reveals secrets is a constant gossip; avoid the one who babbles with his lips.
Whoever curses his father or mother, his lamp will be extinguished in deepest darkness.
An inheritance gained quickly will not be blessed in the end.
Do not say, "I will avenge this evil!" Wait on the LORD, and He will save you.
Unequal weights are detestable to the LORD, and dishonest scales are no good.
A man's steps are from the LORD, so how can anyone understand his own way?
It is a trap for a man to dedicate something rashly, only later to reconsider his vows.

units.label: The glory of youth and age

verses.text: A wise king separates out the wicked and drives the threshing wheel over them.
The {{ner|spirit}} of a man is the lamp of the LORD, searching out his inmost being.
Loving devotion and faithfulness preserve a king; by these he maintains his throne.
The glory of young men is their strength, and gray hair is the splendor of the old.
Lashes and wounds scour evil, and beatings cleanse the inmost parts.

ner.gloss: Lamp, referring in verse 27 to the human spirit as the LORD's own lamp, searching out a person's inmost being. The image ties human self-knowledge to divine illumination, since only the LORD's lamp truly exposes what is hidden in the heart, echoed in verse 20 where a lamp extinguished pictures the ruin of one who curses his parents.

basic.context: Chapter 20 warns against the folly of drink and quarreling, praises honest weights and honest speech, and insists no one can claim a pure heart by his own effort. It ends by tying a king's secure throne, and every person's honest self-examination, to the LORD, whose lamp searches the innermost being.
basic.hermeneutics: These are wisdom generalizations about how honest, sober, patient living tends to go well and how fraud, drunkenness, and self-righteousness tend toward ruin. The chapter is realistic about human limits, no one can honestly say his heart is pure, verse 9, which keeps the proverbs from becoming a boast of self-achieved righteousness.
basic.originalLanguages: The Hebrew ner, lamp, verse 27, pictures the human spirit as a light the LORD Himself has lit to search out a person's inmost being; the same image of an extinguished lamp, verse 20, pictures the darkness that comes on one who dishonors father and mother. The chapter's repeated concern for honest measures, verses 10 and 23, uses commercial language familiar to every marketplace.
basic.typology: Verse 9's honest admission, 'who can say I have kept my heart pure,' anticipates the New Testament's verdict that none is righteous, Romans 3:10, and points toward the need for a righteousness given rather than achieved. The king whose throne is preserved by loving devotion and faithfulness, verse 28, foreshadows the greater King whose throne is established forever in steadfast love.
basic.christ: Verse 9 confesses that no one can claim a pure, cleansed heart, a confession the New Testament sharpens in Romans 3:10 to 23, driving every honest reader to the righteousness God gives in Christ rather than one anyone achieves. And verse 27's picture of the LORD's lamp searching the inmost being anticipates Christ, who knew what was in man, John 2:24 to 25, and whose light exposes and yet also heals what it exposes.
basic.god: God is the maker of both ears that hear and eyes that see, verse 12, the one whose lamp searches every hidden human depth, verse 27, and the one who alone can secure a throne through loving devotion and faithfulness, verse 28. He hates dishonest weights, verse 10 and 23, because His own character is unwavering truth, and so He calls His people to reflect that same integrity in the smallest transactions of daily life.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 3:10-23 answers verse 9's confession that no one has a pure heart. 1 Samuel 16:7 echoes the LORD who searches the heart rather than outward appearance. Psalm 89:14 grounds a throne in loving devotion and faithfulness, as in verse 28. Romans 12:19 echoes verse 22's call to wait on the LORD rather than avenge oneself.
basic.oneStory: Proverbs 20 calls for honest dealing, sober living, and patient trust rather than vengeance, while confessing that no one can honestly claim a pure heart. The Bible's whole story answers that confession in Christ, the King whose throne is founded on steadfast love, whose light searches every heart, and who alone provides the purity no one can achieve for himself.

context.literary:
Proverbs 20 has the look of a loose heap, but two threads hold it together. The first is the lamp. Verse 20 says the lamp of one who curses his parents will be put out in deepest darkness, and verse 27 says the spirit of a man is the lamp of the LORD. The second is the scales. Verse 10 condemns differing weights and measures and verse 23 says nearly the same, so that the two verses bracket the central panel and make dishonest scales the chapter's hinge.

Between the lamp and the scales are small hinges of their own. The chapter begins with the disordered man, wine that mocks and quarrels that burst, and moves steadily inward from conduct to motive. Verse 5 speaks of the 'deep waters' of the heart, verse 9 asks who can say his heart is pure, verse 24 admits that no one can even understand his own way, and verse 27 gives the LORD the lamp that searches 'his inmost being'. The same inward chamber appears again in the last verse, 'beatings cleanse the inmost parts'. The movement is from outside to inside: from what a man does at the market to what only God can see.

The king keeps returning too. Verses 2, 8, 26 and 28 give a small portrait of the good monarch, who frightens the guilty, sifts out evil with his eyes, drives the threshing wheel over the wicked and is preserved by loving devotion and faithfulness. That portrait is hung beside the confession of verse 9, so that even the best king is judged by the God whose lamp is lit in him.
context.historical:
Behind verses 10, 14 and 23 is the open market of an agrarian town. Goods were weighed on balances against stones kept in a bag, and the Hebrew of verse 10 reads literally 'a stone and a stone, an ephah and an ephah', the doubled stones and doubled dry measures of a trader who kept two sets, one heavy for buying and one light for selling. The law had forbidden exactly this, Deuteronomy 25:13 to 16 and Leviticus 19:35 to 36, and the prophets later accused the powerful of 'dishonest scales', Amos 8:5, and the 'short ephah', Micah 6:10 to 11. The buyer in verse 14 who cries 'worthless, worthless' and then gloats is the other half of the same market: the dishonesty of a bargainer who talks down a price he knows is good.

The king in this chapter judges in person. A king 'sits on a throne to judge', verse 8, and the people came to him for justice, as they came to Solomon, 1 Kings 3:28. 'Lamp' belonged to the vocabulary of the royal house, since the LORD promised that David would always have a lamp before Him in Jerusalem, 1 Kings 11:36, and David's men refused to let him risk battle lest 'the lamp of Israel' be put out, 2 Samuel 21:17. The extinguished lamp of verse 20 therefore carries the weight of a family line cut off.

The curse of a parent in verse 20 was a capital matter under the law, Exodus 21:17. Verses 22 and 25 speak to private revenge and rash vows. Vowing was a normal act of Israelite devotion, but it could be disastrous, as the tale of Jephthah warns, Judges 11:30 to 31.
context.canonical:
Verse 9 is answered by the whole of Scripture's doctrine of sin. Solomon had already prayed, 'there is no one who does not sin', 1 Kings 8:46, and Job asks the same question, 'Who can bring out clean from unclean?', Job 14:4. Paul concludes with the verdict 'There is no one righteous, not even one', Romans 3:10, and John says that if we claim to have no sin we deceive ourselves, 1 John 1:8. The remedy is in the same place, because 'if we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us', 1 John 1:9, and the psalmist's prayer 'Create in me a clean heart, O God', Psalm 51:10, begs for what verse 9 says no one can claim.

Verse 27's lamp meets David's own prayer, 'Search me, O God, and know my heart', Psalm 139:23, and the LORD's own words in Jeremiah 17:10, 'I, the LORD, search the heart'. The New Testament says that God's word 'judges the thoughts and intentions of the heart', Hebrews 4:12, and that Jesus 'knew what was in a man', John 2:25. Verse 22 stands behind Paul's 'leave room for God's wrath', Romans 12:19. Verse 10 and verse 23 are the proverb form of the law and the prophets on honest measures, and Jesus' 'with the measure you use, it will be measured to you', Matthew 7:2, borrows the market's language for the moral life. Verse 28 is picked up by Psalm 89:14 and Psalm 61:6 to 7.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The teacher wants a sober life in the open. He starts with the damage wine and quarrels do, because the scenes that follow are mostly public ones: the market, the court, the gate. His main instruction is that honesty is not a private virtue. A merchant's weights, a buyer's talk and a gossip's tongue are all small acts with large effects on a community's trust.

He also means to humble the pupil. Verse 9 is the quiet centre of the chapter's moral argument. After pages of praise for integrity, he asks who can say he has kept his heart pure. The question stops the reader from thinking that the proverbs reward a clean self made by effort. The chapter ends with the lamp of the LORD rather than the resolve of the pupil, which means that the cure for hidden motive is exposure to God.

Last, he teaches waiting. Verse 22 refuses a man the right to say 'I will avenge this evil'. The reader is to hand a wrong to the LORD, and the shape of the chapter makes that reasonable, because the LORD is the one who sees what no court can.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter mixes commands, observations and one confession. Verses 10, 18, 22 and 25 are close to commands: use honest measures, seek counsel, do not take revenge, think before you vow. Verses 4, 13, 17 and 21 are observations that describe how things tend to go, and are not guarantees. A slacker's harvest is empty, fraud tastes sweet and then turns to gravel, a quick inheritance rarely blesses.

Verse 9 is of a different kind, a rhetorical question whose answer is no one. It does not describe a fact that a few meet and most do not. It sets a limit on the whole book.

Verse 30 needs the most care. It describes how pain cleanses, and its words cannot be lifted into a rule for any setting. In an Israelite community without prisons, corporal punishment was a normal public penalty, Deuteronomy 25:1 to 3 limited it, and the rest of Proverbs treats rebuke and instruction as the first remedy. What carries across to us is the principle that consequences teach and that correction is sometimes costly, not a prescription for any particular method of punishment.

debates.question: Is the 'spirit of a man' in verse 27 a lamp that the LORD kindles, or a lamp the LORD uses to search?

views.label: The conscience, lit by God and shining inward
views.case: The BSB footnote offers 'breath or speech' for the word, and the same word is God's gift of breath in Genesis 2:7. On this reading the capacity to know oneself, conscience, is God's lamp in a person, and by it the person is made accountable. Romans 2:15 speaks of a conscience that bears witness.

views.label: The LORD searches by means of the human spirit, not apart from it
views.case: The line says the lamp is the LORD's and it searches. The point may be that the LORD is the one who searches, and the person's own breath and mind are the equipment He uses. This fits verse 24, where a man cannot understand his own way, and verse 5, where intentions are deep water that another must draw out.

debates.bearing: Either way, the lamp is not the person's own possession. A person cannot read his own motives with confidence, verse 9, so the honest response is the psalmist's prayer to be searched, Psalm 139:23 to 24.

debates.question: What does verse 30 say about punishment, and does it still apply?

views.label: It endorses corporal discipline as a cleansing
views.case: Taken at face value, the verse says that blows reach what words do not, and the book speaks of the rod in other places, 13:24 and 23:13 to 14.

views.label: It states that painful consequence can reform, whatever the method
views.case: The Hebrew is compressed and the images vivid. What matters is that the cost, not the instrument, does the cleansing. Elsewhere Proverbs treats rebuke as the first remedy, and Ephesians 6:4 forbids a father to provoke his children.

views.label: It describes the discipline God Himself brings
views.case: Because verse 27 sets the LORD's lamp in the inmost being and verse 30 speaks of the inmost parts, some read the closing verse as a picture of how the LORD's searching, sometimes through hardship, cleans a person within, as in Hebrews 12:11.

debates.bearing: None of the readings makes the verse a command to inflict injury. It states a general truth, that the heart is not reached by comfort alone.

study.originalLanguages:
The two most striking pieces of language in this chapter are about breath and chambers. In verse 27, 'the spirit of a man' translates nishmat adam, and the BSB footnote notes 'breath or speech'. Nishmat is the very word used when God 'breathed into his nostrils the breath of life' in Genesis 2:7, and Elihu uses it too, saying that 'the breath of the Almighty gives them understanding', Job 32:8. The proverb therefore says that the thing God put into the first man is the lamp He now carries into the dark corners of each person.

The 'inmost being' of verse 27 is literally the chambers of the belly, and the phrase returns in verse 30 as 'the inmost parts'. The Hebrew sees the inner life as a house with rooms. The lamp of the LORD goes through them one by one, and verse 30's painful cleansing reaches the same rooms.

Verse 10 is best read in the BSB footnote, 'a stone and a stone, an ephah and an ephah'. The doubling is the sin. It is not that a stone is wrong but that there are two. The Hebrew idiom for a divided heart, 'a heart and a heart', appears in Psalm 12:2, and the double weight is the market form of the same duplicity.

Verse 14 has the buyer say ra, ra, 'bad, bad', or 'worthless, worthless'. The repetition is the buyer's performance, a show of contempt, and the verse comes alive when we see it as comedy. In verse 6 the same chesed that verse 28 says preserves a king is what 'many a man' proclaims, and the sceptical question 'who can find a trustworthy man?' uses a word, emunim, from the root that gives us 'amen'. So the chapter begins with a world full of the word loyalty and short of the thing, and ends with a king whom chesed and faithfulness actually hold up.

Verse 2 has a small footnote in the BSB: 'literally sins against his own soul'. The man who provokes the king does not merely lose his life; the Hebrew says he sins against his own nefesh. Fools harm themselves first.

The verb in verse 28, 'preserve', is natsar, to guard or watch over. It is the verb of 24:12, where the One who guards your life knows what you do. The king is kept by the same guarding the LORD gives a person, and chesed and faithfulness are the guards posted at his throne.

typology.type: The lamp of the LORD searching the inmost being, verse 27
typology.fulfillment: The lamp that searches the hidden rooms of a person is the light of God's gaze. In the Gospels it takes the face of Jesus, who 'did not need any testimony about man, for He knew what was in a man', John 2:25, and who calls Himself 'the light of the world', John 8:12. The escalation is from a searching light to a saving one. The light that exposes is the light of life, and He promises that those who follow will never walk in darkness. The type falls short by itself: it exposes but cannot cleanse, and what verse 9 asks for is a cleanness that only the cross supplies.

typology.type: The throne preserved by loving devotion and faithfulness, verse 28
typology.fulfillment: A king who reigns by chesed and truth is the royal ideal of the Psalms, 'Righteousness and justice are the foundation of Your throne; loving devotion and faithfulness go before You', Psalm 89:14. Every Davidic king fell short. The promise runs on to the Branch who 'will reign wisely as King and will administer justice and righteousness', Jeremiah 23:5, and Hebrews 1:8 hears Psalm 45:6 as spoken to the Son, 'Your throne, O God, endures forever and ever'. The type is fulfilled in a throne no failure of the king can overturn. It falls short because the earthly king needed his lamp tended, and his throne in the end fell.

typology.type: The weights and balances of a righteous judge, verses 10 and 23
typology.fulfillment: The honest scale is an image of the judgment God will carry out with perfect accuracy. 'Honest scales and balances are from the LORD', Proverbs 16:11. In the New Testament God judges 'through Christ Jesus', Romans 2:16, and the One who will do it has Himself borne the weight of what the scales show. The correspondence is between a merchant's honesty and the Judge's. The escalation is that on the cross the scales are met at the point of greatest mercy, and the Judge Himself takes the sinner's side. The picture falls short of the gospel because a balance can only weigh, and weighing cannot forgive.

study.christ:
Proverbs 20 is a chapter about the heart, and it ends by naming the light that sees it. That is where Christ appears.

Start with verse 9, 'Who can say, I have kept my heart pure; I am cleansed from my sin?'. The expected answer is nobody. The New Testament says the same and then adds what the proverb could not: 'God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God', 2 Corinthians 5:21. The impossible cleanness is given as a gift. The question the sage asks, and cannot answer, the gospel answers: Jesus can say it, and by union with Him His people have it.

Then verse 27. The LORD's lamp searches the inmost being. John tells us that Jesus 'knew what was in a man', John 2:25, and that when the true light came into the world people 'loved the darkness rather than the Light because their deeds were evil', John 3:19. What the proverb describes as a lamp becomes a person who walks into the market, the temple and the courtyard of a priest, and the heart is read. The same light that exposes also heals, and Ephesians 5:13 says that everything exposed by the light 'becomes a light itself'.

Verse 28 gives the king: 'Loving devotion and faithfulness preserve a king; by these he maintains his throne.' Christ is the king in whom chesed and faithfulness are not qualities he must work to keep but who He is. 'Righteousness and justice are the foundation of Your throne', Psalm 89:14, and John writes that Jesus came 'full of grace and truth', John 1:14. In Him the chesed that men only proclaim, verse 6, is found.

Finally, verse 22 teaches waiting on the LORD rather than avenging. Peter says that Jesus, when He was reviled, did not revile in return but entrusted Himself to the One who judges justly, 1 Peter 2:23. He is both the example of the verse and the reason his people can obey it. Guard against forcing the other sayings, such as the drinker, the vow and the gray hair, into Christ; they are wisdom for ordinary life, and the gospel is better served by reading the hinge verses closely than by making every line a type.
study.god:
This chapter shows God as the one who sees. Verse 12 says the LORD made both the ear that hears and the eye that sees, and verse 27 says His lamp searches every room of the inner person. Together they are the ground of the whole chapter's ethics. If a man cheats in a market and no court ever catches him, he has still been seen; if a man keeps a sincere intention that no one ever knows, he has also been seen. Psalm 94:9 makes the argument explicit: 'He who affixed the ear, can He not hear? He who formed the eye, can He not see?'

It also shows a God who guides without being understood. Verse 24 says a man's steps are from the LORD, so that no one can fully understand his own way. This is not fatalism. In the same chapter the pupil is told to work (verse 13), counsel (verse 18), wait (verse 22) and not to vow rashly (verse 25). It is a statement that the human story is larger than the human mind, and so humility is the right posture. Proverbs 16:9 holds the same pair: 'A man's heart plans his course, but the LORD determines his steps.'

The chapter also shows a God who cares about arithmetic. Verses 10 and 23 say that differing weights are detestable to the LORD, and the repetition suggests that this is no small matter. God's interest in the market is not a lesser interest than His interest in the temple. A holy God who made ears and eyes is concerned with whether a farmer gets an honest measure of grain. The God of Israel is the God of the scale as well as the altar.

And it shows a God who waits and acts. Verse 22: 'Wait on the LORD, and He will save you.' The patience He asks of us is a patience He practises, and the promise does not mean that the wrong never happens. It means that the one who sees will act, in His time.

For worship, this chapter takes prayer into the open air. It teaches us to pray Psalm 139:23, to ask to be searched, not hidden from, and to give thanks that the One who sees us wholly also keeps faith with the king's throne, the borrower's cry and the cheated buyer.

crossReferences.note: The law behind verses 10 and 23. Two sets of weights, one heavy and one light, and two measures, one large and one small, are forbidden, and the reason is given: dishonesty in these matters is detestable to the LORD. The proverb uses the law's own word for the sin.

Amos pictures merchants who cannot wait for the Sabbath to end so they can sell grain, reducing the ephah, raising the shekel and cheating with dishonest scales. The prophet shows verse 10 at scale: private fraud turned into a pattern of exploiting the needy.

The LORD asks whether He can forget the short ephah and false weights. It joins verses 10 and 23 to the covenant lawsuit, where dishonest commerce is one of the sins for which the city is called to account.

Solomon's prayer at the dedication of the temple admits 'there is no one who does not sin'. It is the royal commentary on verse 9: the king who might be thought to have a clean heart is the first to confess that nobody does.

Paul gathers psalm texts into the verdict that no one is righteous. It answers the rhetorical question of verse 9 with the full weight of the gospel's diagnosis, so that the way is open to the righteousness given in Christ.

David asks the God who knows him to search his heart and test his concerns. It is verse 27 turned into prayer, and it shows the right response to the lamp of the LORD: invite the light, do not avoid it.

The heart is deceitful beyond cure, who can understand it, yet the LORD searches it and rewards according to deeds. It states the problem that verses 9 and 24 sense and the remedy that verse 27 names.
Jesus did not entrust Himself to the crowd because He knew what was in a man. The lamp of verse 27 has become a person whose gaze reads hearts, and who can therefore be trusted with them.
Do not avenge yourselves, but leave room for God's wrath. Paul takes verse 22 and roots it in a quotation from the law, making clear that waiting is not weakness but a trust that God will act.

When you make a vow to God, do not delay, because He takes no pleasure in fools, and it is better not to vow than to vow and not fulfil it. It is the long form of verse 25's warning that a rash vow is a trap.

Righteousness and justice are the foundation of the LORD's throne, with loving devotion and faithfulness going before Him. It lifts verse 28 from the earthly king to the heavenly one, whose throne is preserved by the same two virtues.

study.oneStory:
Proverbs 20 is a chapter about what people hide and what God sees, and the story of the Bible begins with the same two things. In Genesis 3 the man and the woman hid from the sound of the LORD walking in the garden, and He asked, 'Where are you?'. The fall made the human heart a place of hidden rooms. By Genesis 6 the LORD saw that every inclination of the thoughts of the human heart was only evil, and the rest of the Old Testament works out what to do with a race that cannot say, with a straight face, that it has kept its heart pure.

The law gave Israel external standards, honest weights and respect for parents, and the chapter shows how those standards live in markets and homes. The kings were meant to embody them. The Old Testament portrait of a king sifting evil with his eyes and keeping his throne by chesed and faithfulness is a hope more than a record, since the kings in the books of Samuel and Kings repeatedly fail in the very ways the proverb names. Even David, whose lamp the LORD promised to keep burning, had to ask to be searched.

In Christ the two lines meet. The lamp comes into the world as a person, the king who reigns by chesed and truth arrives, and the heart that no one could cleanse is cleansed by His death and His Spirit. Those who belong to Him are told, 'you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord', Ephesians 5:8, and so the lamp of the LORD becomes their lamp too, John 8:12.

The story ends with a city that has no need of lamp or sun, because the Lord God gives it light, Revelation 22:5. Nothing is hidden there because nothing needs to be, the weights are true, no one has to say 'worthless' to haggle, and the throne is secure for ever. The chapter's final picture of a lamp searching the inmost being is answered by a final picture of a people who walk in the light of the One who has searched them and kept them.

quiz.q: What does verse 1 say about wine and strong drink?

options.text: Wine is a mocker, strong drink is a brawler, and being led astray by them is not wise.
options.note: Drunkenness is tied directly to folly and loss of self-control.

options.text: They are always sinful in any amount.
options.note: The verse's specific concern is being led astray, not a blanket prohibition of any amount.

options.text: They make a person wiser through relaxation.
options.note: This is the opposite of the verse's warning.

options.text: They are neutral, with no moral concern attached.
options.note: The verse explicitly calls being led astray by them unwise, so it is not morally neutral.

quiz.q: According to verse 9, what can no one honestly claim?

options.text: That he has kept his heart pure and is cleansed from sin.
options.note: The verse is a rhetorical question exposing universal sinfulness.

options.text: That he has ever sinned at all.
options.note: This reverses the verse's point; it is about the impossibility of claiming purity, not claiming sin.

options.text: That he owns honest weights and measures.
options.note: That theme appears elsewhere in the chapter, verses 10 and 23, but is not the subject of verse 9.

options.text: That he is wealthier than his neighbor.
options.note: Wealth is not the topic; verse 9 concerns the heart's purity from sin.

quiz.q: What does verse 10 say God thinks of differing weights and measures?

options.text: They are detestable to the LORD.
options.note: Dishonest commerce is treated as morally repugnant to God, not merely inefficient.

options.text: They are a minor inconvenience.
options.note: The verse's language, 'detestable,' is far stronger than mere inconvenience.

options.text: They are acceptable if profitable.
options.note: This directly contradicts the verse's moral judgment.

options.text: They are only wrong if discovered by others.
options.note: The verse grounds the wrong in God's own judgment, not merely in being caught.

quiz.q: What does verse 22 counsel instead of personal revenge?

options.text: Wait on the LORD, and He will save you.
options.note: Patient trust in God replaces the impulse to avenge oneself.

options.text: Take swift revenge before the offender escapes.
options.note: This is exactly what the verse forbids.

options.text: Ignore the wrong entirely and pretend it did not happen.
options.note: The verse counsels waiting on the LORD for vindication, not denial of the wrong.

options.text: Seek revenge only through legal channels.
options.note: The verse's counsel is trust in the LORD's action, not merely a legal alternative to personal revenge.

quiz.q: What does verse 27 call the spirit of a man?

options.text: The lamp of the LORD, searching out his inmost being.
options.note: Human self-awareness is pictured as a divine light exposing the heart's depths.

options.text: A flame that burns out with age.
options.note: The verse's emphasis is searching and illumination, not the effect of aging.

options.text: A candle easily extinguished by sin, with no lasting purpose.
options.note: Verse 20 speaks of an extinguished lamp for cursing parents, but verse 27 itself emphasizes the LORD-given searching function of the spirit.

options.text: Something entirely hidden from God.
options.note: The verse says the opposite, that this lamp searches out the inmost being under the LORD.

questions: Verse 1 warns that wine and strong drink lead astray those who are unwise. Where might you need firmer boundaries around anything that clouds your judgment?
Verse 9 asks who can claim a pure, cleansed heart. How does honestly answering 'not me' change the way you view your own righteousness before God?
Honest weights and measures mattered enough to God to be called detestable when corrupted, verses 10 and 23. Where in your work or dealings are you tempted toward small dishonesties?
Verse 22 calls us to wait on the LORD rather than avenge ourselves. What wrong are you currently tempted to repay rather than entrust to God?
The LORD's lamp searches the inmost being, verse 27. What would change if you invited God to examine a part of your heart you usually keep hidden, even from yourself?

translationNotes.note: 'Deep waters' pictures the hidden intentions of the heart as something only patient, discerning listening can draw out, like water drawn from a deep well.
The rhetorical question form, 'Who can say', expects the answer 'no one,' functioning as an implicit confession of universal sinfulness rather than a genuine inquiry.
'The spirit of a man' translates neshamah, breath or spirit, distinct from ruach elsewhere, but both point to the inner life the LORD alone fully searches.
